title: The Unique Challenge of Leading in a Matrix Organization
author: Admired Leadership Field Notes
summary: A primer and argument rolled together. The primer defines the matrix organization: team members report to more than one leader at once, typically a functional leader and a business or regional leader, producing a grid of accountability rather than a single reporting line. The authors then name three variants by which authority is distributed: Weak Matrix (functional leader dominates, project leader has limited authority), Strong Matrix (project leader has primary authority, functional leader handles strategy and resources), and Balanced Matrix (shared authority). Understanding which variant is in operation is the first diagnostic any leader should make, because the way influence flows in the organization depends on it. The argumentative claim is that leading in a matrix is categorically different from leading in a traditional hierarchy. Because leaders share people, decisions, and resources with peers, success depends on influencing without authority, negotiating tradeoffs, and securing buy-in from people who do not formally report to them. Dictating solutions fails. Guiding the group to decisions succeeds. Political and organizational savvy becomes a required skill rather than a bonus. The leader who struggles most is the one who treats the matrix as broken hierarchy rather than as a different system with its own grammar. The piece closes on a specific influence strategy the authors argue is the single highest-leverage move in a matrix: informational power. Unlike expert power (skill-based) or authority power (position-based), informational power comes from gathering and sharing valuable information effectively. Leaders in a matrix become more influential by explaining the why behind requests, supplying timely updates, presenting data that highlights the benefit of a proposed action, marshaling benchmarks and evidence, and positioning themselves as a hub and conduit for the information others need to do their jobs. For a school leader operating in any kind of dotted-line structure (district-and-school, content lead and grade lead, trust and academy) the translation is that becoming the best-informed and most transparent person in the room is itself a leadership act.
points: The central argument of this piece is grounded in the author's engagement with how real people think and act, not in idealized or abstract reasoning.
The takeaway is actionable,it can be implemented at the classroom or school level without waiting for policy change or external resources.
The piece challenges a common default assumption in education practice and offers a concrete alternative framed by evidence or lived experience.
The stakes are clear: what happens if leaders or teachers adopt this approach, and what is the cost of continuing the current default.
quotes: In a matrix organization, team members report to more than one leader or manager at the same time, typically a functional leader and a business or regional leader. This creates a grid-like system of accountability instead of a single straight line of reporting.

A Weak Matrix is where the functional leader dominates, and the project or daily task leader has limited authority. A Strong Matrix is where the project leader has primary authority and the functional leader mainly manages strategy and resource allocation. In a Balanced Matrix, the functional and project leaders share authority relatively equally.

Leading in a matrix organization requires a stronger emphasis on influence, collaboration, and negotiation than a traditional hierarchy. Because leaders share people, decisions, and resources with other leaders, they must resolve conflicting priorities with peers directly.

Success often depends on influencing without authority, negotiating tradeoffs, and securing buy-in from people who do not formally report to the leader. The impact of decisions on other functions, regions, and projects must always take precedence over simply making a call.

Instead of dictating solutions to problems, leaders in a matrix must learn to guide the group to decisions. It takes political and organizational savvy to navigate the formal and informal power structures that reside in the matrix.

Of the many influence strategies critical to effective leadership in a matrix organization, informational power stands out. By gathering and sharing information, leaders show themselves to be credible sources and important to others’ success. Unlike expert power (based on skill) or authority power (based on position), informational power comes from having access to valuable information and using it effectively.

Good leaders in a matrix share information to build trust by explaining the why behind their requests, reducing uncertainty by offering timely updates, presenting data in a way that highlights the benefits of a proposed action, gathering data and evidence to support a plan or strategy, offering insights and perspectives to increase buy-in, and marshaling benchmarks and metrics to make a convincing case.

Leaders in a matrix think of themselves as an information hub and conduit to others. The more information and data they gather and share, the more influential they become.” Archived from Admired Leadership on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
